newsitem.title: FINLAND: Analysts slow to warm to Partek - Sisu deal.
newsitem.headline: Analysts slow to warm to Partek - Sisu deal.

text.p: Investment analysts on Wednesday were waiting to be convinced of the benefits for Finland's Partek Oy in buying state vehicle maker Sisu Oy, saying the logic of the deal was not immediately apparent.
"I think we have seen a lot more logical mergers recently," said analyst Niklas Geust at FIM Pankkiiriliike, adding he was awaiting a conference call at 1730/1530 GMT.

Partek -- a cargo handling equipment and construction materials group -- said it would buy state vehicle maker Sisu Oy in a complex series of deals which analysts said at first sight looked pricey and not a perfect match.
Partek's stock initially rose eight percent on the news but fell into negative territory after analysts' first assessments.
The deal valued Sisu at 46-47 markka per share and was some 10 times 1995 profits and "clearly higher" on 1996 earnings, Geust said. "That looks a little high," he added.

Sisu's 1995 net profit was 150.6 million markka -- 4.07 markka per share -- but in 1996, its January-August pre-tax profit slumped to 15 million from 121 million. This suggested a clearly lower full-year 1996 profit, Geust said.

Asked at a news conference what know-how Partek had that could improve Sisu's recently weak earnings, Partek CEO Christoffer Taxell said: "I think ... it is not fair to say that Sisu's core business has not been strong."
Though some analysts said they had expected the state to float Sisu rather than sell it off to another firm, they admitted they did not yet know the state-owned company well.

"The last person I would have though of Sisu going with was Partek," said another London-based analyst, requesting anonymity until he could form a fuller opinion. He added that he was broadly positive about Partek.
Another analyst, also requesting anonymity, said Partek faced quite a challenge to bring the new group into shape and create a clean, attractive investment prospect.
Partek's statement said there were potential synergies but CEO Christoffer Taxell told a news conference that these would be less than 100 million markka per year.
But analysts were far from explicitly negative.

"I think it could be a welcome change in the sense that Cargotec has always been the most interesting part of Partek and this deal might strengthen it," said Taina Uljas at Barclays de Zoete Wedd in London.
And Harri Laajala at Merita Bank was ready to speak warmly about the plan: "I take a positive view of this," he said, adding: "I see this as a logical step for Partek."
"Partek has consistently said it has certain core businesses -- in other words, Cargotec and minerals -- and now it seems that precast concrete will be allowed to go its own way."
He expected most synergy benefits to come longer-term.
